states.name: Texas
states.deadline_summary: Two years for most cases under Texas law — sometimes less, with special rules for children. In Texas, most injury and medical-malpractice claims must be filed within two years (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §16.003; §74.251), and medical-malpractice cases require a detailed expert report within 120 days (§74.351). Texas also caps non-economic damages in medical-malpractice cases at $250,000 per provider (§74.301); economic damages like medical bills and lost income are not capped.
notes_extra: 60 days' pre-suit notice generally required — §74.051; expert report required within 120 days of filing — §74.351.

states.name: Oklahoma
states.deadline_summary: Two years for most cases under Oklahoma law — sometimes less, with special rules for children. In Oklahoma, most injury and medical-malpractice claims must be filed within two years (Okla. Stat. tit. 12, §95). Oklahoma does not currently cap non-economic damages — the state's $350,000 cap was struck down as unconstitutional in Beason v. I.E. Miller Services (2019).

states.name: New Mexico
states.deadline_summary: Three years for most cases under New Mexico law — sometimes less, with special rules for children. In New Mexico, most injury claims must be filed within three years (NMSA §37-1-8); medical-malpractice cases fall under the Medical Malpractice Act (NMSA §41-5-13), which is largely occurrence-based with special tolling for young children. New Mexico's malpractice cap changes annually and differs for hospitals vs. independent providers, and generally does not limit medical-care benefits or punitive damages.

states.name: Arizona
states.deadline_summary: Two years for most cases under Arizona law — sometimes less, with special rules for children. In Arizona, most injury and medical-malpractice claims must be filed within two years (Ariz. Rev. Stat. §12-542). Arizona is one of the few states whose constitution prohibits caps on injury damages (Ariz. Const. art. 2, §31) — a jury, not a legislature, decides the full value of an Arizona victim's harm.
